To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk models selected a group of 3.2 million people, equal in size to 11% and to the upper 5th of the German population aged 50–80, and that they selected a group with 1.7 million lung cancers, equal in size with 50% of lung cancers in the full German adult population.

the USPSTF eligibility criterion selects a population that is equal in size to about 11% of the adult population aged 50 to 79 and that is equal in lung cancer risk to the upper fifth (20%) of the ever smoking population aged 50–70.

in the German population the USPSTF eligibility criteria would select a group that is equal to the upper fifth (20%) of the population at highest risk of developing lung cancer and that a risk prediction model would select a group of similar size that would include half of the lung cancer cases in the full German adult population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to identify the most appropriate risk model to be used in the German population for screening eligibility.

the question of which risk model is best suited to identify the population at highest risk of lung cancer in the German population and how the results can be used in the context of a screening program.

a major challenge for the implementation of lung cancer screening in Germany, namely how to identify individuals at high enough risk to benefit from screening while minimizing the risk of over-diagnosing and over-treating individuals with indolent lung cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for Germany, risk models would select individuals with higher 5-year lung cancer risk than eligibility criteria, but the latter may still include individuals at elevated lung cancer risk.
risk models are superior to simplified selection criteria for lung cancer screening, and that in Germany the PLCO M20112 is the best model available.
the PLCO M2011 model performs better than any other risk model in the German population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk models are more accurate in predicting lung cancer cases than the eligibility criteria.

in the German population risk models would be expected to select individuals at higher risk of lung cancer, but also to include more older persons and ex-smokers than eligibility criteria based on smoking history.
the PLCO M2011 model is the best available tool for risk assessment for lung cancer in the German population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk prediction models are better suited to identify individuals at elevated risk of lung cancer than the standard eligibility criteria.
, in Germany and probably in other European countries as well, risk prediction models can identify a population at higher lung cancer risk than eligibility criteria based on smoking history.
risk prediction models may help to identify a population with high lung cancer risk that is not captured by the standard eligibility criteria.
